Warm-up and mobility

Clay shooting looks calm: you stand, mount the gun and shoot. Yet over a day of Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting you mount a heavy gun and turn your body many times. Many coaches find that cold muscles make this movement stiff and jerky.

Coaches' experience

A warm-up is light movement before the first round. There is no set length; many coaches suggest about 10 to 15 minutes. The aim is not to get tired but to wake the body up: warm the muscles, loosen the joints and settle your breathing. There is little research on warm-ups in clay shooting, so these tips come from the experience of coaches.

Coaches' experience

Mobility means how freely your joints move: whether you can turn your head, lift your arms and twist your trunk as far as the shot needs, without strain. For a shooter the key areas are the neck (the head comes down onto the stock) and the shoulders (the mount). The upper back and hips turn your body with the target, and the ankles keep you steady in your stance.

Coaches' experience

A simple routine you can do at the ground, without the gun:

  1. Slow head turns and tilts, without fast circles.
  2. Shoulder rolls forwards and backwards.
  3. Trunk turns with your hands on your hips.
  4. A few shallow squats.
  5. Rocking from your heels to your toes.

Coaches' experience

Tip: Repeat each movement a few times, smoothly and without pain. There is no fixed number.

Coaches' experience

Many coaches suggest dynamic exercises before shooting: gentle movements you repeat and make a little bigger each time, like shoulder rolls that grow wider. Static stretching, where you hold one position at its limit for a long time, is usually left for the evening, after shooting.

Coaches' experience

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Mock shooting means mounting and swinging the gun along an imagined target. During a competition it is not allowed anywhere at the ground, so mount the gun only to shoot (Chapter 8 · Mock shooting and accidental shots). Before the event nobody may practise on the competition layouts, so warm-up shooting is done on other layouts (Chapter 15 · No practice on competition layouts).

Compak® Sporting

In Compak® Sporting the rules call this simulated shooting and ban it only in some cases (Chapter 24 · No simulated shooting off the stand; no shooting animals). During a competition you may not mount and swing the gun outside the shooting positions, or while someone in your squad is shooting. Before the event you may practise on the competition trajectories, but with a different trajectory setting table: a ready-made menu that says which traps throw the targets at each station. So during practice you see the same targets, but in other combinations than on the day (Chapter 6 · Practice on competition trajectories). At continental and world championships official practice opens on the Saturday before the championship (Chapter 6 · Championships: official practice from the Saturday before).

For both disciplines many coaches suggest warming up without the gun at a competition. Practise the mount with an unloaded gun (dry mounting) at home or in training, where the law and the ground's rules allow it (Dry practice of the mount).

Coaches' experience

Safety: If you have an injury or long-lasting pain in the back, neck or shoulder, put your routine together with a doctor or physiotherapist. If an exercise hurts, stop: physiotherapists and coaches generally treat pain as a signal to stop, not to push through.

Coaches' experience

Key points

  • Light, dynamic movement before the first round, often about 10–15 minutes
  • Focus on the neck, shoulders, back, hips and ankles
  • Move smoothly and stop if it hurts
  • At a competition, warm up without the gun (Sporting™: no mock shooting at all)
  • Sporting™: no practice on the competition layouts; Compak® Sporting: practice only with another setting table (another menu of traps per station)

Did you know?

A few slow trunk turns between rounds can help too: over a long day the muscles have time to cool down again.

For the interpreter
  • The Compak® Sporting rules say simulated shooting, the Sporting™ rules say mock shooting. Both mean mounting the gun and swinging it along an imagined target, so one term in your language can cover both.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. How long a warm-up do many coaches suggest before shooting?

    1. An hour of hard training
    2. About 10–15 minutes of light movement
    3. A shooter needs no warm-up at all
    Answer

    About 10–15 minutes of light movement

    There is no set length; many coaches suggest about 10–15 minutes of light movement that warms the muscles without tiring you.

  2. Which kind of warm-up do many coaches suggest before shooting?

    1. Long stretches held at the limit
    2. A long-distance run before the round
    3. Movements that grow a little bigger each time
    Answer

    Movements that grow a little bigger each time

    Gentle movements that grow a little each time wake the body up; long stretches held at the limit are usually left for the evening.

  3. Before an ordinary Compak® Sporting competition (not a continental or world championship), may you practise on the competition trajectories?

    1. Yes, but with other trajectory setting tables
    2. No, it is forbidden there as in Sporting™
    3. Yes, with the same tables as the event
    Answer

    Yes, but with other trajectory setting tables

    In Compak® Sporting practice on the competition trajectories is allowed with other setting tables. At continental and world championships official practice opens only on the Saturday before the championship. In Sporting™ nobody may practise on the competition layouts.

    Chapter 6 · Practice on competition trajectories
